goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: Introduce a deliberately defect-graded 2D interlayer at energy-device interfaces so that point-defect density is highest only where trapped water/adlayers must be expelled; this should increase local wettability/friction enough to dewet and immobilize nanometric interfacial films, thereby restoring short-range van der Waals contact and reducing both adhesion loss and defect-driven electrical nonuniformity at the interface.
mechanism: Combines the idea that controlled defect chemistry in graphene-like 2D materials tunes wettability and friction (2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::2, 2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::6) with the finding that ultrathin water/adlayers dramatically increase interface spacing and sharply reduce adhesion/van der Waals stabilization (2609.11459::mechanism_principle::0, 2609.11459::causal_claim::8). Applied to defect-sensitive energy interfaces where minimizing interfacial defects and resistive loss is critical (2609.11755::problem_motivation::4, 2609.11755::constraint::2), the mechanism is that defects alter interfacial liquid affinity and sliding resistance, promoting adlayer breakup/removal and tighter conformal contact, which suppresses interfacial gap defects and contact resistance.
crosses_boundary: Crosses from graphene-water tribology/membrane defect chemistry into epitaxial adhesion physics and then into defect-limited semiconductor/electrode interfaces; the non-obvious step is using defect-controlled wetting/friction not for transport through membranes, but to remove hidden nanometric adlayers that undermine adhesion and electronic stability.

goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: In solid-state metal/2D-coated electrolyte interfaces, defect engineering should be used to raise the exchange current density and homogenize contact only when paired with strong interfacial adhesion and stack pressure; under this combined regime, roughness-induced stress fields are redistributed over a larger real contact area, suppressing defect-centered current hotspots and stabilizing deposition.
mechanism: Mechanical stress and roughness geometry control local current concentration at rough Li/solid-electrolyte interfaces, with defects acting as hotspot nucleation sites and stress becoming most influential when i/i0 is low or pressure/contact quality is high (2609.11571::hypothesis_statement::0, 2609.11571::causal_claim::2, 2609.11571::causal_claim::5, 2609.11571::evidence_result::7). Separately, adlayers weaken adhesion by increasing interface spacing (2609.11459::causal_claim::8). The proposed combined mechanism is that a defect-engineered 2D interlayer can increase interfacial kinetics/selective ion transfer (2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::6) while adhesion control removes weakly bonded gaps; this creates a continuous mechanically coupled interface so applied pressure can effectively flatten stress gradients instead of merely compressing isolated asperities. The result is reduced defect-focused current localization and more stable electrodeposition.
crosses_boundary: Crosses electro-chemo-mechanical dendrite theory in solid-state batteries with 2D defect-controlled interfacial transport and thin-film adhesion physics. It is non-obvious because battery models usually treat mechanics/current distribution, while 2D defect studies focus on wetting/transport rather than using adhesion restoration to make stress stabilization actually effective.

goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: Use a bilayer-function 2D interlayer at the electrode/active-material interface: confine higher point-defect density to an ultrathin outer skin that faces the trapped water/adlayer during lamination, while keeping the remainder of the 2D sheet and the actual electronic contact plane low-defect. This defect-localized skin should raise local wettability/friction enough to break up and pin nanometric interfacial films during assembly, but because the electronically transmitting plane remains comparatively pristine after contact closure, the interface can recover short-range van der Waals adhesion without paying the full penalty of defect-induced scattering, leakage, or chemical instability.
mechanism: The revision addresses the main plausibility concern by spatially separating the two roles that were previously assigned to one defect-graded layer. Prior work suggests defects in graphene-like 2D materials can tune wettability and friction, and that nanometric interfacial water/adlayers greatly increase spacing and sharply weaken adhesion/van der Waals stabilization. Here, defects are not distributed through the whole conducting interlayer; instead, they are concentrated only in the surface region that first encounters residual water/adlayers. During transfer or stack formation, that defective skin preferentially interacts with the liquid film, increasing dissipation and pinning so the film ruptures into isolated patches or is swept toward escape paths, reducing the continuous adlayer that holds the solids apart. Once the adlayer is disrupted, the underlying low-defect basal plane can approach the counter-surface closely enough to restore stronger van der Waals contact and lower interfacial gap density. Because the high-defect region is kept shallow and remote from the final current-carrying contact plane, the design is more plausible than a fully defect-graded conductive interface: it preserves the adhesion-control benefit of defect engineering while limiting added carrier scattering, reactive sites, and leakage pathways that would otherwise worsen electrical nonuniformity. The key testable prediction is that there will be an optimum defect-skin thickness/density window where adhesion retention and contact stability improve while contact resistance does not increase, unlike uniformly defect-rich interlayers.
crosses_boundary: Yes. It still combines 2D defect-tuned wettability/friction concepts with interfacial-adlayer-controlled adhesion physics and applies that synthesis to defect-sensitive energy-device contacts, but now in a more testable architecture that decouples liquid-management defects from the electronic transport plane.

goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: At solid-state metal/2D-coated electrolyte interfaces, the most stabilizing defect strategy is not to maximize defect density, but to create a low-density, spatially isolated population of ion-affinitive defects in a strongly adhered 2D interlayer whose interface spacing is minimized by adhesion control and stack pressure. This regime should raise exchange current density enough to move the interface into the stress-regulated deposition window while keeping defect spacing larger than the stress-current interaction length, so defects act as uniformly distributed ion-transfer relays rather than defect-centered filament nuclei or electronic leakage sites.
mechanism: Roughness and material inhomogeneity generate local normal-stress variations that focus current at protrusions and defects; when i/i0 is low, stress more strongly governs current distribution, so higher i0, lower interfacial resistance, and pressure can suppress hotspot growth by redistributing load and current over larger real contact area (2609.11571::hypothesis_statement::0, 2609.11571::causal_claim::2, 2609.11571::causal_claim::5, 2609.11571::evidence_result::7). The weak point in the original hypothesis is that indiscriminate defect creation could also open fast-filament or electronic-leakage pathways. The revised mechanism therefore requires adhesion-first spacing control: because adhesion decays steeply with increased interface spacing, minimizing spacing via a strongly bonded 2D interlayer removes poorly coupled gaps where isolated asperity compression, parasitic interphase growth, and local field intensification would otherwise occur (2609.11459::causal_claim::8). On that mechanically continuous interface, only a sparse set of controlled defects is introduced to tune wettability/selective ion transfer (2609.11602::hypothesis_statement::6). If defect density is kept below a percolation-like threshold, each defect lowers local transfer resistance without forming a connected electronically conductive or chemically weak pathway; pressure then couples these isolated transfer sites through the adhered sheet, smoothing stress and current between them. The key testable prediction is nonmonotonic behavior versus defect density: stability improves at low-to-moderate isolated defect density but degrades once defects become close enough to interact, percolate, or nucleate filaments.

mechanism: The synthesis is that defect engineering and adhesion control should be spatially co-designed rather than applied uniformly. goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: Use a 2D interlayer with defect chemistry confined to mechanically compressed contact-rim/percolation zones around pre-existing high-gap or high-field asperities, while the load-bearing background remains low-defect and strongly adherent. The defect-rich zones are chosen to be passivated, ionophilic edge/oxo-type sites that lower local adlayer persistence and raise exchange current only where current crowding would otherwise initiate; under stack pressure, these targeted sites should collapse nanometric weak-gap films, expand real contact area, and reduce i/i0 locally enough for stress to suppress rather than amplify deposition heterogeneity. This should improve stability more plausibly than a generic defect gradient because it avoids placing highly reactive defects across the whole interface and makes a clear prediction: there is an optimum areal fraction and placement of passivated defects that minimizes hotspot formation and delamination, whereas too many or misplaced defects will reintroduce parasitic reactions and crack initiation.
mechanism: Adlayers weaken van der Waals adhesion very strongly when their thickness is comparable to the equilibrium 2D-interface gap, so the highest-value intervention is not uniform defect addition but selective modification of the specific weak-gap patches that already trap water/contaminants and concentrate stress/current. In those patches, controlled defects in the 2D layer increase wettability/friction and selective ion transfer, helping immobilize or displace interfacial films under pressure and promoting local contact closure. Because these defect sites are spatially restricted and chemically passivated, they act as interfacial 'activation islands' rather than distributed failure nuclei. Once the weak-gap patches collapse, the surrounding low-defect regions provide the main adhesion and mechanical continuity, so stack pressure is transmitted over a larger real contact area instead of isolated asperities. Electrochemically, the activated islands raise local exchange current density at the places most prone to current crowding, lowering local i/i0 into the regime where stress can homogenize current distribution rather than being overwhelmed by kinetic polarization. The model therefore predicts a non-monotonic dependence on defect coverage: too little targeted defect density leaves persistent adlayers and hotspots; too much spreads mechanical weakness/reactivity; an intermediate, spatially aligned population of passivated defects gives maximal adhesion recovery, lowest current localization, and best cycling stability.

goal: How can defect engineering and interfacial adhesion control be used together to improve stability of 2D materials and electrode interfaces in energy-related devices?
hypothesis: Engineer a 2D interlayer with spatially graded defect density and adhesion: highly defective, wetting/friction-enhanced nanosites are placed only where interfacial water/adlayers and current crowding are likely, while the surrounding area is kept low-defect and strongly van-der-Waals-coupled; under stack pressure this architecture should simultaneously dewet weak-gap regions, restore intimate contact, and redistribute stress/current more uniformly, yielding a stable, low-resistance interface for 2D energy devices.
mechanism: This synthesis couples Branch B’s adlayer-removal concept with Branch A’s stress-electrochemistry stabilization. Controlled defects in the 2D layer locally increase wettability, friction, and possibly ion-exchange/transport, so trapped nanometric water or reaction-derived adlayers are preferentially broken up, immobilized, or expelled exactly at the regions that would otherwise create interfacial spacing defects. Because such adlayers sharply weaken adhesion by increasing separation, their removal restores real contact area and strong short-range van der Waals coupling. The key added element is that once contact becomes mechanically continuous, applied stack pressure no longer acts on a patchy interface but on an adhered one, so stress is distributed more evenly instead of concentrating at isolated protrusions/voids that seed current hotspots. Meanwhile, defect-enabled increases in local exchange kinetics lower effective i/i0 in the problematic regions, making pressure/stress more able to homogenize current and suppress nonuniform deposition or extraction. Thus defect engineering is not used uniformly to add disorder; it is used selectively to clean and activate the interface, while adhesion control preserves a low-defect load-bearing background. The combined result is fewer interfacial gap defects, lower resistive loss, reduced delamination/current localization, and improved operational stability at interfaces such as 2D contacts and solid-electrode junctions.
crosses_boundary: Yes: it bridges nanoscale defect-chemistry/adhesion control at 2D interfaces with mesoscale stress-governed electrochemical current distribution, linking interfacial wetting physics to mechanical-electrochemical stability in energy devices.

A thin adsorbed interfacial film/water layer is present because HI vapor originates from aqueous solution and oxo-group reduction releases water; since this layer is comparable in thickness to the equilibrium graphene–h-CuI gap, it can strongly weaken van der Waals adhesion.

Interfacial adlayers strongly hinder supported h-CuI epitaxial growth because increasing interface spacing causes adhesion to decay steeply, strongly reducing the van der Waals stabilization needed for growth.

Mechanical stress, together with interfacial roughness geometry, critically governs interfacial current distribution and metal electrodeposition behavior in roughened Li/solid-state-electrolyte interfaces.

Surface roughness geometry/material inhomogeneity governs local normal-stress variations, and these stress variations around elongated or extruded protrusions cause localized current concentration and preferential, nonuniform Li deposition/growth; if mechanical stress is neglected, deposition remains nearly uniform even on rough surfaces.

The relative importance of stress versus kinetic/interfacial-resistance effects is controlled by the normalized interfacial current density (i/i0): stress dominates overpotential, current distribution, and electrodeposition behavior when i/i0 is sufficiently low, such as under low interfacial current density, high exchange current density, low interfacial resistance, or high stack pressure; at high applied current density stress can often be ignored unless exchange current density is substantially improved.

Prior literature cited in the paper reported that current concentrates near defects, producing nonuniform normal current density, and that increasing external pressure enhances deposition stability when the shear modulus ratio is low.

Interface defects must be evaluated because interfaces strongly govern carrier separation/extraction and practical devices can contain many defects; the CNGS/MoTe2 interface is a particularly critical engineering target, and minimizing interfacial defects there is necessary to approach predicted performance experimentally.

Approaching the predicted performance experimentally requires controlling absorber quality, minimizing interfacial defects, especially at the CNGS/MoTe2 junction, and reducing parasitic resistive losses.

plausibility_critic.feedback: The hypothesis is broadly physically plausible because spatially selective defects can indeed modulate wettability, friction, adhesion, and local electrochemical kinetics while improved real contact under pressure can reduce constriction resistance and stress/current localization, but its success will depend sensitively on whether the introduced defects avoid causing faster chemical degradation, excessive ion trapping, or loss of mechanical integrity in the 2D interlayer.

novelty_critic.feedback: This is a reasonably non-obvious cross-domain synthesis because it combines localized defect-mediated wetting/adlayer removal with adhesion- and pressure-driven stress/current homogenization into a spatially patterned interface design, rather than merely restating either mechanism alone.

feasibility_critic.feedback: This is realistically testable by combining patterned defect/adhesion engineering with standard Raman/XPS/KPFM, AFM-friction/adhesion mapping, cross-sectional TEM, operando electrochemistry/EIS, and pressure-dependent contact-resistance measurements, though proving the full causal chain between localized adlayer removal, stress redistribution, and current homogenization will require carefully correlated in situ experiments rather than any single routine characterization.
